plan.topic: FDA's class-wide label change (Nov 9, 2026) adding NAION, a rare sudden vision loss, to warnings and precautions for all GLP-1 medicines including tirzepatide, and how it differs from temporary blurry vision
plan.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide and Vision: What the FDA Just Added #shorts', or 'Will Tirzepatide Affect Your Eyes? #shorts'. Open: 'The FDA has added a rare eye condition called NAION to the warnings for all GLP-1 medicines, including tirzepatide. Here's what that means and the signs to know.' Give the absolute rate: about 6 vs 4 cases per 100,000 person-years in pooled trials, GLP-1 medicines vs comparison medicines. Say the FDA notes cases have been reported with every marketed GLP-1. Contrast this without dismissing blurry vision: blurry vision can also happen when blood sugar changes quickly, so any new or changing vision is worth telling your clinician about. Then the FDA signs: sudden painless vision loss in one eye, which you may notice on waking; blind spots or tunnel vision; colours looking off; blurry or hazy spots. Any of these → contact your healthcare professional right away, or your local urgent care or emergency number. Then the scoped don't-stop line, regular eye exams (especially with diabetes), the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line. Source: the FDA DSC only. Use no eye-damage imagery and no smiling or check-mark mascot.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Blurry Vision: Is This Normal? #shorts
plan.why: The radar rates it the top-momentum (95) caution story. Coverage is driven by scary headlines, so a calm, label-first take fills a gap and fits our best Short format. It also updates our 11-09 eye Short, which said the label didn't list NAION. | fact-check: Verified: on 9 Nov 2026 the FDA issued a Drug Safety Communication requiring all GLP-1 RA labels to add NAION to Warnings and Precautions (fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential). Zepbound and Mounjaro are named. Problems in the angle: (1) The FDA does NOT say semaglutide is 'studied most'. It says 'NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products', and its estimate pooled 126 RCTs across multiple GLP-1 RAs: 6.4 vs 3.8 cases per 100,000 person-years (GLP-1 RA vs placebo or non-GLP-1 glucose-lowering medicine). Use that absolute-rate framing instead. (2) 'Most common in adults 50 and over' isn't an FDA claim about risk on GLP-1s. The FDA only gives the background incidence in adults over 50. Drop it, or state it exactly as background incidence. (3) The FDA lists 'blurred or missing portions of vision' and 'reduced central sharpness (e.g., blurry or hazy spots)' as NAION symptoms. So the hook 'Usually it's not what the headlines describe' and the 'Is this normal?' title play down a symptom the FDA says needs prompt action. That's the main safety problem. (4) The FDA's patient action is 'contact their health care professional right away'. Use that wording, and you can add 'or your local urgent care or emergency number' for sudden vision loss. Symptoms: 'sudden, painless vision loss in one eye that patients may notice upon waking' ('may', not 'often'), blind spots or tunnel vision, distortion of colours, blurry or hazy spots. (5) The FDA says people who have had NAION should talk with their health care professional about whether to continue. Keep the scoped don't-stop line. Calling this 'one new fact' is fine for a 13:00-style news fact, but it's in the 08:00 slot, so the title needs the calm 'Will it…?' form without false reassurance.

package.title: Tirzepatide & GLP-1s: FDA's Rare, Possible Eye Risk Warning #shorts
package.description:
The FDA added a warning about a rare, possible eye risk called NAION (an optic nerve condition) to all GLP-1 medicines, including tirzepatide. In 126 pooled randomized trials: about 6.4 cases per 100,000 person-years on GLP-1 medicines vs 3.8 on placebo or other diabetes medicines.

The FDA's signs: sudden, painless vision loss in one eye (you may notice it on waking), blurred or missing patches of vision, distorted colours, less sharp central vision. Contact your healthcare professional right away. Can't reach them? Call your local urgent care or emergency number.

Don't stop, switch or change your medicine on your own.

Source: FDA Drug Safety Communication on GLP-1 RAs and NAION (Nov 2026) https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential

#GLP1 #Tirzepatide #NAION #FDA

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
PASS with one minor fix. I checked every claim against the FDA Drug Safety Communication dated November 9, 2026, and the page is live. It confirms these points:
- The NAION labeling change covers all approved GLP-1 receptor agonists, including Mounjaro and Zepbound.
- The FDA calls the risk "potential" and NAION "rare".
- In a pooled analysis of 126 randomized controlled trials (134,253 patients), there were 6.4 NAION cases per 100,000 person-years on GLP-1 medicines, against 3.8 on placebo or other (non-GLP-1) glucose-lowering medicines.
- "NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products."
- The warning signs are: sudden, painless vision loss in one eye that may be noticed on waking; blurred or missing parts of vision, such as blind spots or tunnel vision; distorted colours; and reduced central sharpness.
- People should contact their health care professional right away.

The script gives the absolute rates, hedges correctly ("rare, possible"), keeps the data at class level ("GLP-1 medicines", not one drug), and lists the safety lines in the right order. The don't-stop line fits the FDA's advice to decide about continuing or stopping together with a clinician. The closing lines are correct, and the Short comes in at about 130 words, well under 170. The one fix: scene s6 leaves out the FDA's word "blurred". Two optional tweaks would also tighten the wording.

issues.problem: The FDA's wording is "blurred or missing portions of vision (visual defects such as blind spots or tunnel vision)". The script drops "blurred", which is the sign viewers are most likely to notice, and it makes blind spots and tunnel vision sound like the whole symptom rather than examples of it.
issues.fix: Narration: "Blurred or missing patches of vision, like blind spots or tunnel vision." List item 2: "Blurred or missing patches of vision (like blind spots or tunnel vision)"

issues.claim: 6.4 on GLP-1s vs 3.8 on placebo/other diabetes medicines (126 trials)
issues.problem: The numbers are accurate. The FDA calls these 126 randomized controlled trials. Adding "randomized" shows the strength of the evidence. This is optional wording polish.
issues.fix: On-screen text: "NAION cases per 100,000 person-years: 6.4 on GLP-1s vs 3.8 on placebo/other diabetes medicines (126 randomized trials)". Narration: "In one hundred twenty-six pooled randomized trials, about six point four cases per hundred thousand person-years on GLP-one medicines. Three point eight on placebo or other diabetes medicines."

issues.claim: Contact your healthcare professional right away, or your local urgent care or emergency number.
issues.problem: "Or your local urgent care or emergency number" is our own help-line addition, not FDA text. The line is still tagged to the FDA source. The craft rules say to keep our own additions out of source attribution.
issues.fix: Split it into two sentences so the FDA tag covers only the first: "Contact your healthcare professional right away." (fda-dsc-naion-2026) "If you can't reach them, call your local urgent care or emergency number." (no source tag). Apply the same wording to the on-screen text.
